name: Hofstadter's Law
statement: It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's Law.
statementAccent: even when you take into account
meaning: Estimates run long, and knowing that they run long does not save you — you pad the estimate and it still runs long.
mechanism: Estimating a task means modelling it, but the model omits the very surprises — the unknown unknowns — that eat the time. You cannot budget for what you cannot foresee, and the law's self-reference means even your correction gets absorbed: pad the estimate and the padding, too, is swallowed.

examples.text: A team estimates two weeks for a migration, then doubles it to four 'to be safe'. It ships in seven. The padding was applied to the work they could foresee; the overrun came from the certificate renewal, the flaky test, and the one colleague who alone understood the old schema being on leave.

Planned to open around 1963, it finally opened in 1973 — roughly a decade late, with costs escalating many times over. It is the textbook megaproject illustration of the planning fallacy the law captures.

One of the cleanest documented overruns: forecast at £320 million, the line came in at £776 million and years late. Its very predictability made it the first practical test case for reference-class forecasting.

variants.name: The planning fallacy
variants.text: The empirically-studied cousin, named by Kahneman and Tversky (1979): people underestimate how long their own tasks will take even when they know similar past tasks ran long. Where Hofstadter's Law is a joke, this is the measured phenomenon underneath it.

whyItMatters: The joke has teeth: the fix is not more introspection but outside data. Estimate from how long comparable work actually took, not from how long this work feels like it should take, and treat schedule buffers as a floor rather than a ceiling.

working.text: base the forecast on how long a class of similar past projects actually took — reference-class forecasting — not on how long this one feels like it should.
breaking work into named pieces surfaces the steps a single gut estimate silently drops, and reduces (though never removes) the underestimate.
padding applied to the work you can foresee is swallowed by the work you can't; hold the buffer as a minimum, not a ceiling you expect to keep.
assume some of the schedule will go to problems you cannot yet name, and protect slack for them explicitly.

limits: Hofstadter's Law is a self-referential adage, not a formula — it makes no numeric prediction and is deliberately un-actionable (any correction you apply is, by its own terms, underestimated too). The rigour lives in the planning fallacy beneath it, studied by Kahneman, Tversky, Buehler and others, and in the debiasing methods that genuinely reduce the error — reference-class forecasting, the outside view, unpacking tasks. So the 'even when you account for it' fatalism is rhetorical, not literal: the overrun can be shrunk. The bias is also specific to the forecaster's own upcoming work; detached observers tend to over-estimate instead.
misreadings: It is a wry observation about planning under uncertainty, not a mandate to inflate estimates without end (the self-reference makes that futile). Nor does it claim every task overruns by the same amount — it says complex, novel work resists its own forecasts. The practical reading is to plan for discovery, not to abandon planning.
origin: Douglas Hofstadter stated it in his 1979 book Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (p. 152), in a discussion of how repeatedly people underestimated when a computer would beat the best human chess players. The law is deliberately self-referential, in keeping with the book's preoccupation with self-reference and strange loops.

sources.text: Hofstadter, D.R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. New York: Basic Books. p. 152.
